items.prompt: What is a 'probability distribution'?
choices: A description of how likely each possible outcome of a random process is
A list of every value a variable has actually taken so far
A guarantee that all outcomes will occur equally often
A single number summarizing the most likely outcome only
items.explanation: A probability distribution assigns a likelihood to every possible outcome, which is what lets 'how much variation is normal' be answered with a number instead of a guess.
items.reference:
Probability distribution
🎲 Likelihood of each outcome
📏 Turns "is this normal?" into a number
Why: it replaces a gut feeling about spread with a calculable answer.

items.prompt: According to L1, why can't 'is this uneven?' alone answer whether a random process is broken?
choices: Because even a truly fair process produces uneven-looking results over a finite number of trials
Because unevenness is always a sign of a bug
Because random processes are never actually random
Because probability distributions only apply to computer-generated randomness
items.explanation: L1's key point is that unevenness is normal at finite sample sizes — the real question is whether it's uneven by more than chance alone would produce.
items.reference:
Probability distribution
🎲 Likelihood of each outcome
📏 Turns "is this normal?" into a number
Why: it replaces a gut feeling about spread with a calculable answer.

items.prompt: What does a 'uniform distribution' mean?
choices: Every outcome in a fixed set is equally likely
The outcome is always the same value
Outcomes get more likely the closer they are to the mean
Outcomes are equally likely only if there are exactly two of them
items.explanation: Uniform means no bias toward any one outcome — every outcome in the set has the same probability.
items.reference:
Uniform distribution
⚖️ Every outcome equally likely
🖥️ Example: random server pick
Why: it's the baseline case where no outcome is favored.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, if a load balancer picks uniformly among 4 servers, what is the probability any single server gets picked on one request?
choices: It depends on which server it is
items.explanation: Uniform over 4 equally-likely outcomes means each one has probability 1/4 = 25%, by definition.
items.reference:
Uniform distribution
⚖️ Every outcome equally likely
🖥️ Example: random server pick
Why: it's the baseline case where no outcome is favored.

items.prompt: What does a 'binomial distribution' describe?
choices: The count of successes across a fixed number of independent yes/no trials, each with the same probability
The exact outcome of a single random event
A distribution with exactly two equally likely outcomes
The average value of a continuous measurement
items.explanation: Binomial specifically counts successes over repeated independent trials — it's about how many times something happens, not what a single trial looks like.
items.reference:
Binomial distribution
🔁 Count of successes over N trials
🚦 Example: request failures
Why: it answers "how many times," not "which outcome."

items.prompt: In L1's second scenario, what real-world example is used for the binomial distribution?
choices: How many of the next 500 requests fail, if each has a 2% independent chance of failing
Which of 4 servers a request gets routed to
The exact latency of a single request
Whether a deploy succeeds or fails, a single time
items.explanation: L1 uses request failures across many trials — a count of successes/failures over repeated independent events is exactly what the binomial distribution models.
items.reference:
Binomial distribution
🔁 Count of successes over N trials
🚦 Example: request failures
Why: it answers "how many times," not "which outcome."

items.prompt: What is the 'Central Limit Theorem'?
choices: The tendency for a sum of many independent, small random effects to look normally distributed, regardless of each effect's own shape
A rule stating all real-world measurements are normally distributed
A theorem that only applies to values that are already bell-shaped
A method for computing exact probabilities from a normal distribution
items.explanation: The CLT is specifically about sums of independent effects converging toward a bell curve, even when none of the individual effects are bell-shaped themselves.
items.reference:
Normal distribution / CLT
🔔 Bell curve from summed effects
⏱️ Example: end-to-end latency
Why: it explains why bell curves show up even without a single "naturally normal" cause.

items.prompt: According to L1, why does end-to-end request latency often end up looking normally distributed?
choices: It's the sum of many independent, small delays, and the CLT applies to that kind of sum
Because network latency is inherently bell-shaped on its own
Because servers are designed to enforce a normal distribution
It doesn't — latency is never normally distributed in practice
items.explanation: Latency is a sum of many independent small delays (DNS, handshake, hops, processing) — exactly the setup the Central Limit Theorem applies to.
items.reference:
Normal distribution / CLT
🔔 Bell curve from summed effects
⏱️ Example: end-to-end latency
Why: it explains why bell curves show up even without a single "naturally normal" cause.

items.prompt: What does 'standard deviation' measure?
choices: How much a random quantity typically varies around its mean
The single most likely outcome of a random process
The total number of possible outcomes
Whether a distribution is uniform or not
items.explanation: Standard deviation quantifies typical spread around the mean — it's what turns 'is this far from expected?' into a specific number.
items.reference:
Standard deviation
📐 Typical spread around the mean
🚩 Outlier = several stddevs away
Why: it's the number that distinguishes normal spread from a genuine outlier.

items.prompt: According to L1, what distinguishes a genuine outlier from normal random spread?
choices: A result several standard deviations away from the mean
Any result that isn't exactly equal to the mean
A result that happens more than once
There's no way to distinguish them
items.explanation: L1 explicitly frames a genuine outlier as several standard deviations from the mean — a small deviation is normal spread, not evidence of a problem.
items.reference:
Standard deviation
📐 Typical spread around the mean
🚩 Outlier = several stddevs away
Why: it's the number that distinguishes normal spread from a genuine outlier.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, what is the formula for a binomial distribution's mean (expected count)?
choices: n × p
n / p
√n
items.explanation: The expected count of successes across n independent trials, each with probability p, is n × p.
items.reference:
Binomial formulas
Mean = n × p
Stddev = √(n × p × (1−p))
Why: these two numbers are what let a count be judged as normal or suspicious.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, for n=500 and p=0.02, what is the standard deviation of the failure count?
items.reference:

items.prompt: According to L2, what makes a failure-count alert threshold 'defensible' rather than arbitrary?
choices: It's set far enough past the expected mean and typical spread that crossing it is genuinely informative, not just noise
It's set to the smallest number that could possibly happen
It's set exactly equal to the mean, so any deviation triggers it
Any round number works equally well as a threshold
items.explanation: L2 frames a defensible threshold as one set well past the distribution's natural spread — close to the mean and it fires on ordinary noise, far enough and it actually signals something real.
items.reference:
Setting a threshold
🔔 Too close to mean → noisy alerts
🎯 Far past spread → genuinely informative
Why: the whole point of a threshold is separating signal from ordinary variance.

items.prompt: According to L2, is a failure count within one or two standard deviations of the mean remarkable?
choices: No — that's what independent chance produces on its own
Yes — any deviation from the exact mean is remarkable
Yes, but only if the count is even
It depends on the day of the week
items.explanation: L2 states plainly that a count within one or two standard deviations is unremarkable — it's ordinary variance, not a signal of a problem.
items.reference:
Setting a threshold
🔔 Too close to mean → noisy alerts
🎯 Far past spread → genuinely informative
Why: the whole point of a threshold is separating signal from ordinary variance.

items.prompt: According to L2's flowchart, what's the key insight about summing 6 independent uniformly-spread delays?
choices: The sum tends toward a bell-shaped distribution, even though none of the individual delays are bell-shaped
The sum is always exactly uniform, just like each individual delay
The sum becomes unpredictable and has no describable shape
The sum only looks normal if each delay is already normal
items.explanation: This is the Central Limit Theorem's core claim — summing independent effects produces a bell shape regardless of each individual effect's own distribution.
items.reference:
CLT flowchart
6 flat delays → sum → bell curve
Why: the individual shape doesn't matter — only independence and enough of them.

items.prompt: According to L2, why do normal distributions show up constantly in systems work?
choices: Because many measured quantities are sums of many independent small effects, and the CLT applies to those sums
Because computers are designed to generate normally distributed data
Because every individual delay in a system happens to be bell-shaped
They don't — normal distributions are actually rare in systems work
items.explanation: L2 explains this directly — the CLT means sums of independent small effects look normal even without any single 'naturally normal' cause, which describes most aggregate systems metrics.
items.reference:
CLT flowchart
6 flat delays → sum → bell curve
Why: the individual shape doesn't matter — only independence and enough of them.

items.prompt: According to L2, when independent quantities are summed, what adds up directly?
choices: Their variances (not their standard deviations)
Their standard deviations directly
Neither their means nor their variances
Only their means, never their variances
items.explanation: L2 explicitly notes that means and variances of independent sums add directly — standard deviations do not add directly, since stddev is the square root of variance.
items.reference:
What adds when summing
✅ Means add directly
✅ Variances add directly
🚫 Stddevs do NOT add directly
Why: this is what lets latency budgets be reasoned about from their parts.

items.prompt: Why does knowing that means and variances add directly matter for latency budgets, per L2?

It means latency can never be predicted before deployment
It only matters for uniform distributions, not normal ones
It has no practical use — it's purely a mathematical curiosity
items.explanation: L2 ties this directly to practical use: knowing how component delays combine lets you predict aggregate latency behavior from its parts.
items.reference:
